title: JSON Encoding & Decoding
summary: Go's `encoding/json` turns structs into JSON (`Marshal`) and JSON into structs (`Unmarshal`) using **struct tags** to control field names and behavior. The rules that trip people up are clear once learned: only **exported** fields are encoded, tags like `omitempty` and `-` shape the output, and decoding into `interface{}` makes every number a `float64`.

subtopics.title: Marshal and Unmarshal
subtopics.explanation: json.Marshal(v) returns the JSON encoding of v as []byte; json.Unmarshal(data, &v) parses JSON into the value pointed to by v. Unmarshal needs a pointer so it can store the result. Both return an error you must check — the two calls that anchor everything else in this topic.

subtopics.title: Struct tags control field names
subtopics.explanation: By default JSON keys are the Go field names. A `json:"name"` tag renames the key; this is how you map Go's CamelCase to JSON's snake_case. Tags also carry options after a comma, like omitempty — the phrasebook mapping your struct to the wire format.

subtopics.title: Only exported fields are (de)serialized
subtopics.explanation: encoding/json uses reflection and can only see EXPORTED (capitalized) fields. Lowercase fields are silently ignored on both Marshal and Unmarshal — a very common 'my field is missing/empty' bug, and the first thing to check when a value won't round-trip.

subtopics.title: omitempty and the - tag
subtopics.explanation: `json:"foo,omitempty"` omits the field from output when it holds its zero value (0, "", nil, false, empty slice/map). `json:"-"` excludes a field entirely from both encoding and decoding (e.g. secrets) — the tag options that shape and secure your output.

subtopics.title: Streaming with Encoder/Decoder
subtopics.explanation: json.NewEncoder(w).Encode(v) writes JSON directly to an io.Writer, and json.NewDecoder(r).Decode(&v) reads from an io.Reader — ideal for HTTP bodies and large streams, avoiding buffering the whole payload in memory. This is the form you reach for in real services rather than Marshal/Unmarshal on []byte.

subtopics.title: Numbers decode to float64 in interface{}
subtopics.explanation: JSON has a single number type, so decoding into interface{} (or map[string]interface{}) makes EVERY number a float64 — large 64-bit integers silently lose precision. Decode into a typed struct with an int64 field, or use Decoder.UseNumber() to get json.Number, to keep exact integers. This is the classic untyped-decode gotcha.

foundations.overview: JSON is the lingua franca of web APIs, and Go's standard encoding/json package makes converting between Go values and JSON straightforward — once you know its rules. You annotate structs with tags to control the wire format, and you marshal to bytes or stream through an Encoder/Decoder. The recurring gotchas are reflection-driven: only exported fields are visible, tags govern names and emptiness, and untyped decoding turns numbers into float64.
foundations.formalDefinition: encoding/json provides reflection-based serialization (Marshal) and deserialization (Unmarshal) between Go values and JSON text, with per-field behavior controlled by `json` struct tags and the json.Marshaler/Unmarshaler interfaces.
foundations.whyItMatters: Almost every Go backend service speaks JSON over HTTP. Knowing the tag rules, the exported-field requirement, and streaming with Decoder is essential for correct, efficient APIs and is a standard interview topic.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of struct tags as a translator's phrasebook: the Go struct is your internal vocabulary, the JSON is the external language, and the `json:"..."` tags are the phrasebook entries mapping one to the other. Only words you've made public (exported fields) appear in the conversation.
foundations.runtimePerspective: Marshal/Unmarshal use reflection to walk the value's fields, reading struct tags to decide keys and options. Reflection means only exported fields are accessible. Unmarshal into interface{} produces dynamic types: objects become map[string]interface{}, arrays []interface{}, and ALL numbers become float64 (JSON has one number type). For exactness with big integers, use json.Number via Decoder.UseNumber().
foundations.realWorldUsage: Decoding HTTP request bodies, encoding API responses, reading config files, message-queue payloads, and persisting documents.
foundations.businessImpact: A correct, stable JSON contract is the public API of a service; tag mistakes break clients and cause integration incidents. Streaming decode reduces memory and latency at scale.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Struct tags make the wire format explicit and reviewable; custom Marshaler/Unmarshaler lets you encode domain types (money, time formats) cleanly. Forgetting to export a field is a frequent, confusing bug.
foundations.performanceImpact: Reflection-based encoding is convenient but not the fastest; streaming with Encoder/Decoder avoids buffering whole payloads, and for hot paths teams sometimes use code-generated codecs. Decoding numbers as float64 can silently lose precision for large 64-bit integers.
commonUseCases: Hiding secrets with json:"-" and trimming output with omitempty

commonMisconceptions.reality: Only exported (capitalized) fields are; unexported fields are silently skipped on Marshal and Unmarshal.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Numbers decode to int by default.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Decoding into interface{} makes every JSON number a float64; use a typed struct or json.Number for integer precision.
It needs a pointer (&v) to store the decoded result; passing a non-pointer returns an error and changes nothing.

config.intro: Decoding JSON into a struct, step by step:

steps.name: Pass a pointer
steps.detail: You call json.Unmarshal(data, &v) — the pointer lets json write into your value.

steps.name: Reflect over fields
steps.detail: json walks v's exported fields, reading each field's `json` tag to learn its JSON key.

steps.name: Match keys
steps.detail: For each JSON key it finds the matching field (case-insensitive fallback), ignoring unknown keys by default.

steps.name: Convert & assign
steps.detail: It converts each JSON value to the field's Go type, calling a custom UnmarshalJSON if the type defines one.

steps.name: Leave zero values
steps.detail: Fields with no matching JSON key keep their zero value; an error is returned only on type mismatches or malformed JSON.

visualExplorer.title: Marshaler / Unmarshaler interfaces
visualExplorer.caption: A type can customize its JSON by implementing json.Marshaler (MarshalJSON) and json.Unmarshaler (UnmarshalJSON) — the encoder checks for these interfaces before falling back to reflection.

interactiveExamples.title: Round-trip a struct through JSON
interactiveExamples.explanation: Tags rename fields to snake_case; omitempty drops the empty Email. Note Marshal returns []byte and an error you should check.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: fix the field that never decodes
interactiveExamples.explanation: The price field stays 0 after decoding because it's unexported, so encoding/json can't see it. Make it work by exporting the field and tagging it.

checkpoints.explanation: age is unexported (lowercase), so encoding/json cannot access it and silently omits it — the tag on an unexported field has no effect. Only name appears.

checkpoints.prompt: What is the dynamic type of n?
checkpoints.code:
var v interface{}
json.Unmarshal([]byte(`{"n": 42}`), &v)
m := v.(map[string]interface{})
n := m["n"]
fmt.Printf("%T\n", n)
checkpoints.explanation: Decoding into interface{} makes every JSON number a float64 (JSON has a single number type). To preserve integer precision use a typed struct field or Decoder.UseNumber() to get json.Number.

checkpoints.prompt: Unmarshal returns an error and the struct stays empty. Why?
options: Unmarshal needs a pointer: pass &u, not u
checkpoints.explanation: Unmarshal must receive a pointer so it can store into your value. Passing u by value returns 'json: Unmarshal(non-pointer ...)'. Use json.Unmarshal(data, &u).

checkpoints.prompt: Stream-decode the HTTP request body into req.
checkpoints.explanation: json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&req) streams from the io.Reader without buffering the whole body. Unmarshal needs []byte (not a reader), NewEncoder is for writing, and json.Decode isn't a function.

codeLab.title: Parse a config with defaults and a hidden secret
codeLab.instructions: Define a Config struct and implement `Parse(data []byte) (Config, error)` that decodes JSON into it. Requirements: JSON keys are snake_case (host, port, api_key), Port must default to 8080 when the key is absent, and a malformed JSON input must return a non-nil error.
hints: Set defaults by initializing the struct (Port: 8080) BEFORE Unmarshal; Unmarshal only writes keys present in the JSON.
Tag fields to map snake_case JSON keys (json:"api_key") to exported Go fields.
Return the zero Config and the error on failure so callers can detect bad input.

debuggingLab.title: Marshal produces an empty object
debuggingLab.symptom: json.Marshal of a populated struct returns {} or drops fields, even though the values are set.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The fields x and y are unexported (lowercase), so encoding/json's reflection cannot read them and they are omitted entirely. The struct tags are ignored because the fields aren't accessible. The result is an empty object {}.
commonMistakes: Naming struct fields in lowercase and expecting them to serialize.
Assuming a json tag can expose an unexported field.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Export the fields (capitalize them) and keep the json tags for the desired key names.

theory.question: How does encoding/json decide which struct fields to serialize, and what role do struct tags play?
theory.directAnswer: It uses reflection, so it can only see EXPORTED (capitalized) fields — unexported fields are silently skipped. By default the JSON key is the field name; a `json:"name"` tag overrides the key, and options after a comma (omitempty, the special `-`) control whether and how the field appears. Marshal turns the value into JSON bytes; Unmarshal needs a pointer to store into.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Reflection-based field mapping governed by `json` struct tags.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To let one struct map cleanly to an external JSON contract without manual encoding code.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: json walks exported fields, reads tags for key + options, and (de)serializes accordingly; unexported fields are invisible to reflection.

theory.whyImportant: The exported-field rule and tag options are constant sources of bugs and a standard interview question.
theory.realWorldExample: Mapping Go's CreatedAt time.Time to JSON "created_at" via a struct tag in an API response.

followUps.question: What does omitempty do?
followUps.answer: Omits the field from output when it holds its zero value (0, "", nil, false, empty slice/map).

followUps.question: How do you completely exclude a field, e.g. a password?
followUps.answer: Tag it json:"-", which removes it from both encoding and decoding.

theory.question: What happens when you Unmarshal JSON into an interface{}, and why can that be a problem?
theory.directAnswer: Decoding into interface{} yields generic Go types: JSON objects become map[string]interface{}, arrays become []interface{}, strings string, booleans bool, null nil, and ALL numbers become float64. The problem is precision and ergonomics: large 64-bit integers lose precision as float64, and you must type-assert everything. Decode into a typed struct, or use Decoder.UseNumber() to get json.Number, to avoid this.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Untyped decoding into the empty interface.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To handle arbitrary/unknown JSON shapes when no struct is available.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: json maps each JSON kind to a default Go type; numbers default to float64 because JSON has a single number type.

theory.whyImportant: The float64 surprise causes real integer-precision bugs and is a frequent interview gotcha.
theory.realWorldExample: An ID like 9007199254740993 read into interface{} loses precision; a struct with an int64 field or json.Number preserves it.

followUps.question: How do you preserve integer precision for unknown JSON?
followUps.answer: Use json.NewDecoder(r).UseNumber() so numbers decode as json.Number, then call .Int64() or .Float64() as needed.

followUps.question: When is interface{} decoding still appropriate?
followUps.answer: For truly dynamic/unknown payloads or passthrough; otherwise prefer a typed struct.

theory.question: How do the json.Marshaler / json.Unmarshaler interfaces work, and what is json.RawMessage used for?
theory.directAnswer: A type can implement MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) and UnmarshalJSON([]byte) error to fully control its own JSON representation. Before falling back to reflection, encoding/json checks whether the value (or a pointer to it) implements these interfaces and, if so, calls them. This is how you encode domain types cleanly — a time.Time in RFC 3339, or a Money type as a decimal string. json.RawMessage is a []byte alias that implements both interfaces as an identity: it captures raw JSON verbatim during decode and re-emits it untouched during encode, which lets you defer or partially decode a payload.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two interfaces that let a type override the default reflection-based (de)serialization, plus RawMessage for deferred/partial decoding.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Domain types often have a canonical external format (money, timestamps, enums) that struct tags alone can't express, and sometimes you need to decode only part of a document up front.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The encoder/decoder type-asserts for json.Marshaler/Unmarshaler and delegates to them; RawMessage's MarshalJSON returns the stored bytes and its UnmarshalJSON copies the input, so it acts as a passthrough hole in an otherwise typed struct.

theory.whyImportant: Custom marshalers are the idiomatic way to encode domain types, and RawMessage is the standard tool for envelopes and polymorphic payloads where the concrete type is decided by another field.
theory.realWorldExample: An event envelope struct with a Type string and a Payload json.RawMessage: you decode the envelope once, switch on Type, then Unmarshal the RawMessage into the concrete event struct.

followUps.question: Should MarshalJSON have a value or pointer receiver?
followUps.answer: If the method has a pointer receiver, only *T (not T) satisfies json.Marshaler, so marshaling a non-addressable T won't call it — use a value receiver for MarshalJSON when you want it to apply to both, and a pointer receiver for UnmarshalJSON since it must mutate.

followUps.question: How does RawMessage help with polymorphic JSON?
followUps.answer: Capture the variant payload as RawMessage, inspect a discriminator field, then Unmarshal the RawMessage into the concrete type chosen at runtime — avoiding a two-pass decode of the whole document.

theory.question: How do you decode untrusted JSON safely, and what do DisallowUnknownFields, MaxBytesReader, and UseNumber each protect against?
theory.directAnswer: Use a json.Decoder rather than Unmarshal on unbounded input and layer three defenses. Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields() rejects payloads containing keys that don't map to a struct field, catching typos and preventing silent acceptance of unexpected data. http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, limit) caps how many bytes can be read from the request body, preventing a huge or slow body from exhausting memory. Decoder.UseNumber() makes numbers decode as json.Number instead of float64, preserving exact 64-bit integer precision. Together they bound size, tighten the contract, and keep numbers correct.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A hardened decode path for input you don't control, combining strictness, size limits, and numeric precision.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Default decoding is lenient and unbounded — it ignores unknown keys, buffers whatever it's given, and coerces numbers to float64, all of which are hazards for public endpoints.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: MaxBytesReader wraps the reader and errors past the limit; the Decoder reads from it, DisallowUnknownFields sets a flag that turns unexpected keys into an error, and UseNumber changes number handling to json.Number so no precision is lost.

theory.whyImportant: Public APIs face malformed, oversized, and precision-sensitive input; these three settings turn a naive Decode into a defensible boundary and are common interview and code-review points.
theory.realWorldExample: A signup handler wraps r.Body in http.MaxBytesReader with a 1 MB cap, builds a json.Decoder with DisallowUnknownFields(), and rejects requests with extra or misspelled fields before they reach business logic.

followUps.question: Why not just json.Unmarshal(io.ReadAll(r.Body))?
followUps.answer: ReadAll buffers the entire body first with no size limit, so a malicious client can send gigabytes and exhaust memory; MaxBytesReader plus a streaming Decoder bounds it.

followUps.question: How do you detect trailing garbage after a valid JSON object?
followUps.answer: After Decode, call dec.Decode(&struct{}{}) again and require it to return io.EOF; anything else means there was extra data in the stream.

scenario.question: Your API endpoint sometimes returns a password field in its JSON response, and a downstream consumer's integer IDs occasionally come back wrong. How do you fix both?
scenario.directAnswer: For the leaked password, tag the field json:"-" so it's never serialized (or keep secrets out of the response struct entirely). For the wrong integer IDs, the values were almost certainly round-tripped through interface{} or a float64, losing precision on large 64-bit integers — decode into a typed struct with int64 fields, or use Decoder.UseNumber() / json.Number to preserve exact integers.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two classic JSON contract bugs: accidental field exposure and number precision loss.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Default marshaling serializes all exported fields; untyped numbers default to float64.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: json:"-" excludes a field; typed int64 fields or json.Number avoid the float64 conversion.

scenario.whyImportant: Leaking secrets and corrupting IDs are real, high-severity production incidents.
scenario.realWorldExample: A user object reused for both DB and API leaked its hashed password until tagged json:"-".

followUps.question: Better than json:"-" for secrets?
followUps.answer: Use a separate response DTO struct that simply doesn't contain the secret, so it can't leak by accident.

scenario.question: An API endpoint reuses the database User model as its JSON response, and it just leaked a PasswordHash field to clients. What is the fix, and why is a separate DTO safer than tagging the field json:"-"?
scenario.directAnswer: The immediate stop-gap is to tag the sensitive field json:"-" so it's never serialized. The durable fix is to introduce a dedicated response DTO — a struct that contains only the fields the API is meant to expose — and map the domain model into it before encoding. A DTO is safer because it's allow-list by construction: any field not deliberately added is absent, so a future engineer who adds a new secret column to the DB model can't accidentally expose it. With json:"-" the response is deny-list: it leaks by default and stays safe only if everyone remembers to tag every new secret.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A choice between hiding fields on a reused model (deny-list) versus defining an explicit response shape (allow-list).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Reusing one struct for persistence and transport couples two contracts, so schema changes silently change the wire output.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A DTO decouples them: you construct UserResponse{ID: u.ID, Name: u.Name} from the domain User, and only listed fields ever reach the client regardless of how the domain model grows.

scenario.whyImportant: Accidental exposure of secrets or PII is a high-severity incident, and the allow-list DTO pattern structurally prevents the most common cause.
scenario.realWorldExample: A team splits User (with PasswordHash, internal flags) from UserResponse (id, name, email); the mapping function is the single audited boundary, and adding a new DB column no longer risks a leak.

followUps.question: How do you keep DTO mapping from becoming error-prone boilerplate?
followUps.answer: Write a small explicit toResponse(u User) UserResponse function and unit-test it; avoid auto-copying tools that would reintroduce the reuse problem, and review the mapper as the exposure boundary.

followUps.question: What if the same field must be hidden in some responses but shown in others?
followUps.answer: Use distinct DTOs per view (e.g. PublicUser vs AdminUser) rather than conditional tags, so each endpoint's contract is explicit and independently reviewable.

systemDesign.question: Design the JSON boundary for a Go HTTP service: how would you structure request/response handling so the API is safe, efficient, and evolvable?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Define explicit request and response DTO structs separate from domain and DB models, so the wire contract is intentional and internal fields can never leak. On the way in, wrap the body in http.MaxBytesReader, build a json.Decoder with DisallowUnknownFields(), decode into the request DTO, then run validation before touching business logic. On the way out, map the domain result into a response DTO and stream it with json.NewEncoder(w).Encode. Use streaming Encoder/Decoder rather than Marshal/Unmarshal for large bodies to avoid buffering. Version the contract (URL or media-type versioning) and treat any tag or field change as potentially breaking. Never serialize secrets: allow-list via DTOs, not json:"-" on reused models.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An architecture where the JSON contract is a first-class, isolated layer between the network and the domain.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Coupling the wire format to internal models causes leaks, precision bugs, memory-exhaustion risks, and breaking changes that ripple to clients.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Handlers own DTOs and validation; a mapping layer converts to/from domain types; decoders are size-bounded and strict; encoders stream; and versioning plus explicit DTOs make evolution controlled and secrets structurally excluded.

systemDesign.whyImportant: The JSON boundary is the public API of the service; getting its structure right prevents security incidents, contract drift, and scaling problems all at once.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A payments service exposes /v1/charges with a ChargeRequest DTO (bounded, strict-decoded, validated), maps to a domain Charge, and returns a ChargeResponse DTO with Money serialized via a custom marshaler — internal ledger fields never appear on the wire.

followUps.question: How do you evolve the contract without breaking existing clients?
followUps.answer: Add new optional fields (safe), never repurpose or remove existing ones; for incompatible changes introduce a new version (e.g. /v2 or a new media type) and run both until clients migrate.

followUps.question: Where does validation belong relative to decoding?
followUps.answer: Decode into the DTO first (structural correctness), then run semantic validation on the DTO before mapping to domain types, so malformed and invalid inputs are rejected at the boundary with clear errors.

coding.question: Implement a generic DecodeStrict[T any](data []byte) (T, error) that decodes JSON into a value of type T using a json.Decoder with DisallowUnknownFields, returning a wrapped error on failure.
coding.thoughtProcess: I want one reusable helper that decodes into any target type while rejecting unknown fields. Generics let the caller pick T (e.g. a request DTO) and get back a typed value. I declare a zero value of T, take its address so the Decoder can write into it, build a Decoder over a bytes.Reader, call DisallowUnknownFields(), and Decode. On error I wrap it with %w so callers can still errors.Is/As the underlying decode error, and I return the zero value so a failed decode never yields a half-populated struct.
coding.lineByLine: var out T declares the zero value of the caller-chosen type. json.NewDecoder over a bytes.Reader lets us configure decoding options that plain Unmarshal doesn't expose. dec.DisallowUnknownFields() turns any JSON key without a matching struct field into an error. dec.Decode(&out) needs a pointer, so we pass &out. On failure we return a fresh zero value (never a partially filled struct) and wrap the error with %w so callers can unwrap it via errors.Is/As; %T records which type failed to decode.
coding.timeComplexity: O(n) in the size of the JSON input.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) for the decoded value and decoder buffers.

followUps.question: How would you also bound input size for untrusted callers?
followUps.answer: Decode from an io.Reader instead of []byte and wrap it in http.MaxBytesReader (or io.LimitReader) before building the Decoder, so oversized bodies error out instead of buffering.

followUps.question: Why return the zero value rather than the partially decoded out on error?
followUps.answer: A failed strict decode may have populated some fields before hitting the bad key; returning zero prevents callers from acting on inconsistent, partially-filled data.

coding.question: Implement a custom MarshalJSON for a Money type (cents as int64) that serializes as a decimal string like "12.34".
coding.thoughtProcess: Implement the json.Marshaler interface by giving Money a MarshalJSON() ([]byte, error) method. Format the cents as dollars.cents and return it as a quoted JSON string. encoding/json checks for the Marshaler interface before falling back to reflection, so any struct containing a Money will use my formatting automatically.
coding.lineByLine: Money is an int64 count of cents. MarshalJSON satisfies json.Marshaler. We split off the sign, then format the whole-dollar part (c/100) and the two-digit cents (c%100 with %02d for leading zero). Wrapping in escaped quotes makes the output a JSON string like "12.34". Because the type implements Marshaler, json.Marshal of any struct containing a Money uses this method.

followUps.question: How would you decode it back?
followUps.answer: Implement UnmarshalJSON: strip the quotes, split on '.', and combine dollars*100 + cents into the int64.

followUps.question: Why not store Money as a float64?
followUps.answer: Floats can't represent many decimals exactly, causing rounding errors in money; integer cents are exact.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Define explicit request/response DTO structs at API boundaries rather than reusing domain or DB models, so the wire contract is intentional and secrets can't leak. Version your JSON contracts and treat tag changes as breaking changes for clients.
productionDeepDive.performance: Use json.NewEncoder/Decoder to stream large bodies instead of buffering with Marshal/Unmarshal. Reflection-based encoding is fine for most services; for extreme hot paths, code-generated encoders (e.g. easyjson) or avoiding interface{} reduce allocations and CPU.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: json.Marshal/Unmarshal are safe to call concurrently on different values, but a single Encoder/Decoder bound to one stream is not — use one per request/connection.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Always check the error from Marshal/Unmarshal/Decode. Apply defaults before Unmarshal (it only writes present keys). Consider Decoder.DisallowUnknownFields() to reject unexpected keys when validating strict input.
productionDeepDive.observability: Log decode errors with context (which field/endpoint) but never log raw bodies containing secrets. Track decode error rates as a metric to catch client contract drift.
productionDeepDive.security: Exclude secrets with json:"-" or separate DTOs; never serialize internal fields by accident. Bound request body size (http.MaxBytesReader) before decoding to prevent memory-exhaustion attacks, and use DisallowUnknownFields for untrusted input.

caseStudies.problem: Reusing DB models as API responses leaked internal/secret fields.
caseStudies.solution: Dedicated response DTOs and json:"-" on sensitive fields.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Extra mapping code vs. a safe, intentional contract.
caseStudies.lessons: Separate the wire model from the domain model to prevent accidental exposure.

caseStudies.problem: Integer IDs and money lost precision after JSON round-trips through float64.
caseStudies.solution: Typed int64/Money fields, json.Number via UseNumber(), and custom Marshalers.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly more code for exact, correct numbers.
caseStudies.lessons: Never trust default float64 number decoding for 64-bit integers or currency.

keyTakeaways: json.Marshal encodes a value to JSON bytes; json.Unmarshal decodes JSON into the value behind a pointer (&v) — always check the error.
Only exported (capitalized) fields are (de)serialized; struct tags rename keys and add options like omitempty (drop zero values) and `-` (exclude entirely).
Decoding into interface{} makes every number a float64 — use typed structs or json.Number (Decoder.UseNumber) to keep 64-bit integer and money precision.
Stream large payloads with json.NewEncoder/Decoder, separate wire DTOs from domain models, and bound/validate untrusted input (MaxBytesReader, DisallowUnknownFields).
